utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids welcome to everybody present in the courtroom. I would like to bid welcome to the representatives of the Prosecution, Defence, the two accused, and everybody who assists us in our work, the usher, the registrar, the court reporters, the interpreters, and everybody else inside and outside the courtroom. Before we begin, I have a few issues to raise: Firstly, the Chamber would like to raise the problem arising from the fact that we finished yesterday around quarter past 7.00. As you already know, the plan is fixed in the following way: There is a session in the morning starting at 9.00 and ending at quarter to 2.00, and the afternoon session that begins at quarter past 2.00, which is supposed to finish at 7.00. If we're late in the morning, this has repercussions on the afternoon session, because for technical reasons there is a half an hour delay between the two sessions, and that's why the afternoon session is delayed. And this might pose -- be a problem for the Judges and everybody else. In order to avoid that, we have to adhere strictly to the decisions that have been taken, meaning that the session has to finish either quarter to 2.00 or at 7.00 in the afternoon. Unfortunately, we were from time to time obliged to overstep that time for certain reasons. The Chamber is of the opinion that it has authorised the prolongation of certain sessions because the witnesses had to return to their homeland; they could not stay any longer. And if on Friday we have a witness and if that witness cannot finish on that day, this witness has to stay for three additional days. For this reason, I am appealing to both parties to adhere strictly to the rules. Why? We have noticed - and we discussed that early this morning - that when we overstep the time, this is due to the objections that arrive from one party or the other, and these objections are usually the cause of this problem. And the objections are of two types: The first type of objection that usually comes from either the Prosecution or the Defence arises from the fact that the Defence tends to ask leading questions. Sometimes it is useful, but the Chamber can quote you a number of times that you asked leading questions. In order to avoid that, the Chamber from now on asks you when you are engaged in examination-in-chief or when you ask additional questions, to ask neutral questions rather than leading questions, because the Prosecution will rise and object to any leading questions. The Chamber has stated on various occasions that you have asked leading questions, that those have been objected to. In order to avoid losing and wasting time, we would like to ask you to adhere strictly to the rule that applies to the examination-in-chief and not ask leading questions. We will observe -- we will make sure that this rule is observed. As far as the Prosecution is concerned, we have noticed that the Defence has objected on several occasions regarding new documents which are shown to the witness either in order to test the credibility of the witness or to refresh their memory. Since the Chamber has already indicated, you have the right to do it but before you show a new document to the witness, you have to prepare the grounds by asking pertinent questions because if you want to test his memory or to test the credibility -- refresh his memory or test the credibility, you don't have to show him documents immediately. Showing him the document is your ultimate resource. So if you want to produce a new document, you have to first ask questions that will make the witness either confirm what happened or why he changed his opinion, and then if he does change his opinion, then you can confront him with that contradiction or you can give him the document to refresh his memory. And this was the nature of the objections put forth by the Defence. If you have adhered strictly to the instructions, we will have -- we would have saved time. This week the Judges have not had the time to put questions to any of the witnesses because we did not have the time, and this is not something that should be tolerated. In the future, I am going to ask you, Defence, when you have your witness, I'm going to ask you exactly how much time you will need for the examination-in-chief, and if you go beyond your time, I will have to interrupt you and I will have to cut your examination-in-chief short. If you tell me 45 minutes, it cannot be 50 minutes. Yesterday I asked Mr. Bourgon how much time he would need. He said 45 minutes, and he took an hour. So he went 15 minutes longer. And that is why we had to go beyond 7.00 in the afternoon. A suggest on my part would be when you prepare your examination-in-chief, it's up to you. It's up to the strategy that you have adopted. I believe that it would be useful if you start with the more important questions at the beginning and then -- and leave minor issues for the end. But if you start with the issues of minor importance, sometimes you will not have enough time to put the most important questions. So it makes sense to start with more important things and to finish with things that are not that important. The Chamber believes that if we all respect the rules, we will be able to finish at the time we're supposed to finish. Then we have also to deal with the documents that arise from the testimony. Yesterday we had a new document, so every time we have about half an hour, that we have to take after the testimony. So if you take an hour and a half for the examination-in-chief, if the Prosecution takes an hour and a half, we cannot squeeze everything into the time that we have for one session. When you tell me, "I need an hour and a half," sometimes you won't be able to do everything because of the time that we -- the time constraints that we're facing. Sometimes you -- there are questions that are repetitive and the time could be better used for more fundamental questions. This is in the interest of both parties and in the interest of justice. I'm sure that both parties will make an effort. Both parties have to be aware of that problem because only if we deal with this problem, we will be able to work more efficiently and finish on time. Having said that, before I give the floor to the Defence - because I know that they want to say something - I have to deal with another problem, and that is interpretation or translation. The Judges have made a list of problems linked with the translations contested by the Defence. We have seen that there are six documents. I'm going to give you their numbers. The first one is P662, 429, DH1360, DH270, DH165, and P545, and P616. As regards the document P662, this document is being re-examined by the CLSS as per our decision and the transcript page is 1534. We have received -- as soon as we receive a memo from the CLSS, we are going to ask Mr. Registrar to give us the number. The next document is P429. This document has been admitted as C3. But when this document was shown to Mr. Husic, it didn't refresh his memory at all. He wasn't able to comment on any of the events he was asked about in the document. It is only his testimony that is evidence in the case, and since he was not able to give any testimony having looked at the document, it didn't remind him of anything, in our submission there's no need to have the document marked as a -- a P-number. It will appear on the record that he was shown a document. The relevant portions of the document were read out to him. And that is in our view sufficient for -- for the record. The document could be given a P-number if -- if it had refreshed his memory in some way and it would be necessary to refer to the document in the future. But in our view, as it took the matter no further, it should not be given any identification number at this stage. It may be in the future that in document is to be introduced, but not at this point in our submission. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS

utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, what position did you hold and where were you based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was an officer of the federation army -- or rather, of the ABiH in the course of the war. In 1992, I was the commander of the Zenica Municipal Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you obtain a rank of any kind? And if so, what rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the end of my military career, I obtained the rank of brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or a national court with regard to the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've testified before the Zenica local court. I testified in the Hakanovic case, which had to do with the events in Dusina. That was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you testified in that case, as far as you can remember, were you a witness for the Defence or for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure. I was supposed to testify as to whether Mr. Hakanovic was a member of my military unit and as to whether he could have received orders of any kind from me in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemnly declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence, whom you have already met, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that will be followed. Initially you will have to answer the questions put to you by the Defence for about an hour and 15 minutes. You will notice that the questions put to you will be neutral and not leading, and you might have to provide more less lengthy answers to the questions put to you. Once this stage has been completed, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will also put questions to you. They will conduct what we call their cross-examination, which should take as long as the examination-in-chief. You will notice that the questions put to you in the course of the cross-examination differ from those put to you in the course of the examination-in-chief. When you are cross-examined, you may be asked leading questions, so-called leading questions. In such cases, the witness might be able to answer the questions just by saying yes or no. Once this stage has been completed, the Defence may ask you additional questions that relate to questions put to you in the course of the cross-examination. Defence counsel will be putting neutral questions to you in the course of that stage too. Then the Judges sitting before you may also ask you questions, which will either relate directly to your testimony, and we'll put such questions to you because we feel it is necessary to clarify some of your answers, or because we believe that when answering the questions put to you by both parties certain issues might have been omitted and these issues should be addressed in the interest of justice. When we ask questions, when the Judges ask questions, you shall answer them. Once we have asked our questions, the parties can take the floor again and ask you questions that relate to the Judges' questions. This guarantees that the rights of the parties are respected, in particular the rights of the Defence, which is the party that has called you here. They can put questions to you to correct -- or to ask you to make certain corrections, amendments, provide certain clarifications, et cetera. So roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding. If you fail to understand the sense of a question, ask the party putting it to you to rephrase it because perhaps you're not aware of the fact, but we have no written documents that concern your testimony. This is why your oral testimony is that important. Whatever you say will be interpreted into English, and you will see that there is a screen in front of you in which everything that is said -- on which everything that is said is recorded. There are two other issues I would like to point out to you: Firstly, you have taken the solemn declaration, which means that you should not give false testimony. False testimony is an offence that can be punished and a witness could be given a prison sentence of up to seven years for having given false testimony. In addition, there is another provision contained in the Rules that I should point out to you: If a witness believes that an answer he provides to a question may subsequently be used against him, in such a case the witness can refuse to answer the question. However, this is quite exceptional, and to date we have never had such cases. But if such a case should arise, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question. Nevertheless, the Chamber grants the witness a form of immunity and the witness's testimony can't be used against him. This is a rule -- this is a provision contained in our Rules to ensure that the testimony can proceed as smoothly as possible. If you encounter any difficulties in the course of these proceedings, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. We will have to have a technical break after one and a half hour -- after one and a half hours. You will also find it necessary to have a rest because answering questions can be tiring. So it is also necessary for you to recover and it's also necessary for the interpreters to have a rest. It's also necessary to change the audio CD. This is how we will be proceeding and there shouldn't be any problems. All the previous hearings have run very smoothly. I will now give the floor to Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Saric. I'd be grateful if you could briefly pause after I have put my questions to you. This will give the interpreters time to interpret my question and your answer and it will enable the Chamber and my colleagues to follow you. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, what were you by profession before the war?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Before the war, I was a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What rank did you hold and did you leave the JNA at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Up until the beginning of the war, in Bosnia and Herzegovina I held the rank of captain, and in April 1992 I left the JNA from my service post in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge, you said that in 1992 you were the commander of the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff. Could you tell me: When were you appointed to the Municipal TO Staff in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which organ was above the Municipal TO Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: There was some confusion at the time, but I was appointed by the commander of the Regional TO Staff, and at that time, according to the former laws, the then-War Presidency also had some authority over the Municipal TO Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, did these relations change in accordance with the new rules and were any other units of the ABiH established in the territory of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Towards the beginning of November 1992, a team of officers arrived from Sarajevo and they started forming the corps command and they started organising units that were to become part of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, could you briefly tell us about the general and military situation in Zenica at the time.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, towards the end of 1992, the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was quite intense. That means that combat activity was ongoing in marginal areas and in particular there was combat that resulted in the expulsion of inhabitants, and as a result many refugees arrived in Zenica. The situation in Zenica at the time was very chaotic, very confused, and as I said, it was very chaotic. As far as the town of Zenica itself is concerned, there was a War Presidency which is -- which was a civilian body at the time. It was in session on a daily basis and it would take certain civilian decisions. Apart from the War Presidency of Zenica Municipality, war presidencies -- or rather, the civilian organs of power from other municipalities had more or less moved into Zenica. They had been expelled from their territory. For example, they were from the municipalities of Doboj, Banja Luka, and from many other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, when you became the commander of the Municipal TO Staff, how did that staff function and how many units were under the staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: At the time, the Municipal Staff in fact had two types of units. We had a total of about 130 of various kinds of units, but we only had direct command over a fraction of those units. In fact, we had units to which we only provided logistical support. We did not have command over them. Such units were the Zenica Brigade, the HVO, the HOS, the Green Berets, the Patriotic League, et cetera. And we had direct command only over units that were part of our structure. These were detachments and units attached to the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, tell me how the units over which you in fact had no command, how did these units get established and who in fact had authority over them?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, since the ABiH did not come into existence in a systematic way and in fact there were no legal warehouses, there were no legal means to train and equip these men, and since it was necessary to organise the men in various ways, various units were established in various neighbourhoods, in various areas, and various interests were at stake. Various groups of people would form units, and it depended on how they were able to obtain weapons. As a rule, weapons were bought.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, tell me, what was the atmosphere like in Zenica when Enver Hadzihasanovic arrived there from Sarajevo with a group of officers and started to establish the 3rd Corps command there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation he found in Zenica was extremely complicated to say the least, and for him as a member of the military, it was certainly an atmosphere that was difficult to understand, since in the marginal areas of Zenica there was intense fighting at the time and since there was fighting in other battlefields, it was necessary for him to engage certain units. And when he saw a list of those units, he could see that there were a lot of them. However, when he tried to use those units, that is when he realised that in fact those units weren't present. They'd been organised who knows how and where. And, secondly, he realised it was very difficult to -- for him to use them without the approval of someone who had in fact established them. So that I remember very well that he couldn't understand that some people who had cevapcici shops - these are meat finger shops - had formed units and he had to ask them whether he could use their units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, tell me, what sort of measures were taken by the corps command to introduce order in the situation in that area and to make sure that the army could function properly?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, after having examined the situation and after having put everything down on paper, an attempt was made to form a proper military corps. An order was drafted according to which the 3rd Corps should be formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, tell me, did the formation of the corps and the brigades within the corps have an effect in some way on the organisation and competence of the Municipal TO Staff?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally it did. In the first stage, we received a very serious superior command. There was a chain of command that had been established and gradually we became fully separated from the municipality and we gradually started to rely on the corps command. For a certain period of time we continued to receive logistics support from Zenica municipality and from the War Presidency, and then as the corps command became better organised, the corps took over those responsibilities and we tried to obtain logistics support through the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, tell me, what sort of staff did the Municipal Staff have at its disposal and what sort of staff did the corps have at its disposal towards the end of 1992 and at the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure how correct -- how correctly I can answer this question, but when I arrived -- when I was appointed as the commander of the Municipal Staff, we had about 3.000 men and a third of them had weapons of some kind. As for professional soldiers, well, you could have counted them on the fingers of your hands. Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic encountered a similar situation. It was as if the Presiding Judge in this court was a lawyer and everyone else was -- and everyone else were welders and it was necessary -- and it's necessary for the court to function somehow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the corps was formed and you said that this affected the organisation of the Municipal Staff, which units remained under the control -- under the command of the Zenica Municipal TO?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: When the 3rd Corps was formed, the Municipal Staff -- or the military organisation of the Municipal Staff became fully clear. We had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. three combat detachments and the men in those detachments were elderly men, men who were not very fit, and locally-based men. We had a few service units, communications, logistics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were the main tasks your detachments had? How many such detachments did you have and what were their main tasks?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, the detachments had an unfortunate name: Anti-sabotage detachments. However, in fact these people just secured the territory, and our main task was to provide security in the area and to ensure that the other units could carry out their tasks without having to worry about what was happening in the rear. Taking care of the civilians was also one of the tasks -- or taking care of a certain civilian element, such as the water supply, the electricity, the post office services, bridges, tunnels, important crossroads, et cetera. Taking care of these elements was also one of the tasks that had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, given the new organisation, did you in the Municipal TO Staff have a military police force?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: No. As far as security is concerned, we did not have anyone. We only had two or three men in the Municipal Staff command who were responsible for security issues. And since we were in the town of Zenica, whenever it was necessary to involve the police in something, we would contact our superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although your anti-sabotage detachments had the tasks that you have just described, could you tell me whether you at the time participated in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally the situation throughout the battlefield was very difficult and complicated. Once the Municipal Staff was reorganised, it remained partially armed and partially organised. And in spite of the poor structure, the poor qualifications of the members of the Municipal Staff, we also had to carry out combat tasks in the territory of Zenica municipality and beyond. We were constantly engaged in combat operations with a unit in the Serici sector. We were engaged in a defensive action there. And we would sometimes send a unit to Maglaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned all the units that you were not able to command, you mentioned the HVO too, the Croatian Defence Council. At the time the corps was established and your staff was restructured, what happened to the HVO in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: At that time, the HVO was establishing its Jure Francetic Brigade. And it was at that time that the brigade was indeed established and lined up, the Jure Francetic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under whose command -- under whose command was this brigade? Was it under the command of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Of course not. It was under the command of the Central Bosnia Operation Zone and partly it relied on the logistical support of the town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were the commander of the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff, can you tell me how were you treated by the HVO? Were you considered an HVO ally or was it something else that spoke to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: The situation was a bit funny. The HVO relied on the support from Zenica municipality via the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff. They were even paid through the municipality. However, we could never rely on them. They were not our open enemy in the town of Zenica; however, there was nothing to point to the fact that they were our allies either. Actually, we had a lot of problems with HVO members because all this time they tried to fence off the Croatian territory from the other parts of the town. They did so by setting up checkpoints and by controlling the passage of everybody, both of the members of the army, as well as of civilians. Every day you could see them entering public institutions and companies in the territory of the town of Zenica with the intent to take them, to occupy them and to stay in them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will be using a certain number of documents with this witness, and that's why I would kindly ask the usher to distribute the binders that we have prepared for our learned friends and for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, can you please look at documents after number 25, 26, 27, 28, and 29. I'm going to ask you a question based on documents starting with 25, ending with the last document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: 25, this DH43; DH46, DH44, DH49, and DH50. Mr. Saric, have you seen these documents before? Did you see them at the time when they were drafted?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Of course I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The documents that are now before you, do they reflect what you knew at the time? Do they reflect the way the HVO behaved in Zenica towards the end of 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I have to say that I had a lot of conversations with the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade and we discussed the problems in the territory that I have just described. Those problems were the checkpoints, the control of the territory, the fact that the HVO would storm into companies, seize vehicles and other equipment. Whenever I raised that issue, he would tell me that it was the problem of individuals who did not obey orders and some groups who were just passing through and who were not under his control and command. However, these documents show that it was an organised job and a job well synchronised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, you have told us that your anti-sabotage units provided security for some very important features, such as bridges and crossroads. How did you treat the Lasva junction? Did you consider the Lasva junction a facility of particular significance for that area?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: The Lasva junction at the time was not a significant facility in local terms only. It was a facility of strategic significance for the entire state. Because if the traffic had been interrupted, at that junction the free territory would have been totally fragmented and it would have been practically -- practically impossible to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, in January 1993 did you have any information about the events in the general region which pointed to the specific military significance of the Lasva junction?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, there were several incidents that took place: One in Gornji Vakuf, and some others in some other places. It seemed at the time that these incidents would continue, and having been aware of the fact that the HVO intended to gain control over the most significant facilities and whenever they do control things, that meant trouble for us. That is why we tried everything possible to keep that facility in our hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, can you please look at the document number 4, DH1724 is the number that that document bears, and also document number 3, bearing number 1717. Both documents are in B/C/S only. That's why I would kindly ask you first to look at document number 4 and tell us who was it who issued that document; what does the document represent; also, whether you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: This document was sent by my command to the Regional Territorial Defence Staff of Zenica, because at that time the chain of command did not go directly to the corps command. In the Regional Staff, there is still a few people left and the whole staff was phasing out, but we had to communicate with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read item 1, paragraph 2 and tell us whether this paragraph reflects the positions of your detachment in the period in the territory of Zenica. Can you please read out loud, since we do not have an English translation of this text. Start with: "The Maglaj front line ...."

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: "A shift of 85 military recruits has returned from the Maglaj theatre. A second shift consisting of 60 military conscripts has gone there and they're all on the strength of the 2nd PDO," which stands for the "anti-sabotage unit."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Unit stationed?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Anti-Sabotage Unit was deployed in the western part of the municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any previous tasks with regard to the Lasva junction?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Its zone comprised from the area from the Lasva junction to the Ovnak -- correction, to the Vjetrenice hill. However, the main facility in that zone for which they provided security was the Lasva junction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This shows that a number of military conscripts were engaged in an entirely different area. Did this diminish or, in other words, did this have an impact on the capabilities of the Municipal Staff to perform the task that it was entrusted with?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: If you look at this figure, the figure being 85 military conscripts, that left the Maglaj theatre and the 60 that have replaced them, the difference may not seem that big. However, this was -- this accounted for 70 per cent of the armed members of the army. So when these men carrying arms left the theatre, the unit was reduced to the level of practically not being usable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, can you please look at document number 3, bearing number 1717. Again, tell me who the source of the document is; do you recognize this document; and can you please read item 2.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: This document was sent by the assistant commander for intelligence of the Municipal Staff, and it says here: "Based on the work of the intelligence services and the Anti-Sabotage Units, it has been established that on the 12th January 1993 three buses carrying special units of the HVO from Grude arrived and these forces clashed with the units of the BiH army in the Gornji Vakuf sector. The goal of these conflicts was to disturb the population, to take over power, to control the roads in Gornji Vakuf and Travnik, and to reduce the joint defence efforts against the aggressor."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This type of intelligence that you had at the time, did it prompt you as commander to ask for some sort of intervention from your superior commands?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions, we asked for assistance because we were aware of the importance of the Lasva junction. Unfortunately, on several occasions these cries for help were to no avail. Finally, as the situation developed and as some units became free, we were reinforced for the performance of this task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what -- what it means when you say "we were reinforced"? Were some units resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: An anti-aircraft defence unit was resubordinated to us, as well as one company of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and the main objective was for them to join our units and to provide security for the Lasva junction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 5, bearing number P310. Tell me whether you recognise this document and whether this document confirms the fact that the unit that was resubordinated to you is the one that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document informing the corps command that these units had arrived and that they had been sent to perform their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, the -- the events that followed in the territory around the Lasva junction, did they call for some other defence activities? If that was the case, can you please tell me what was going on in the immediate vicinity of the Lasva junction that prompted you to react?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: At that time, our assumptions that the situation would become more complicated came true. The road towards Busovaca was no longer passable. And due to the HVO checkpoints in the territory, the roads were off limits to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any other additional orders? With this regard, can you please look at documents number 6 and number 7.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Probably because of all these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript - I apologise - the document number 6 bears number P210 and document number 7 bears the number 1726.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: The corps command realised the danger for this part of the territory as the situation developed. It realised that the junction was at risk as well as some roads in the territory. And that is why it issued an order to provide security for the road Zenica-Lasva-Dusina-Sudine and that this road should be kept passable for our units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What about document P1726, number 7?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: This document is me issuing an order to the command of the 2nd Anti-Sabotage Unit. In other words, I conveyed the order of the corps command for this task to be carried out, and the task was to provide security for the road and make it passable for our units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of orders are these? In other words, the command of the 3rd Corps or you yourself, did you ever issue an order for the -- for your units to be used in combat or did you ever issue an order for attack?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Looking at the general -- the overall situation, one could say that our army was in a very difficult position and that for us every bullet and every litre of fuel was very important. We had a number of unpleasant situations with the HVO, but the express order that we received was always that we should grin and bear it because the situation would be resolved at a higher political level and that we shouldn't use force. And this is just one of the orders from the set of orders which were issued in order to prevent what we refer to as "incidents."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, can you please look at document number 9, bearing number 1727. Look at item 3 of this document. Before that, tell me whether you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an order on full combat readiness of the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at item 3. Does item 3 reflect what you have just been testifying about, that units must not be engaged unless attacked?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. You can see that this item shows that I issued an order that authorisation must previously be given if units are to be engaged. No one ever gave such authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saric, could you now tell me whether -- could you tell me what sort of news you started receiving in the Municipal Staff over the following days and in particular on the 26th of January.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Since this unit was sent up there to make sure that the road remained open and a detachment of ours was sent there with the same task, we were expecting this road to remain open. However, I received information according to which there had been some sort of incident up there between the two sides and that people had been killed and wounded in the incident on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at documents under number 10, 11, and tell me -- and have a look at P251. I apologise. I don't have the number P251 in your series of documents. I don't have that document included in the bundle, so I'll ask for this document to be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you show the witness P251.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you to have a look at document number 10, DH1735, and then document number 11, number 1737, and document P251 that has just been given to you. Could you tell me whether this is the information you had on the situation that developed on the 25th and 26th of January in the territory of the Lasva junction?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: This is a report from the corps command to the Supreme Command Staff. Naturally, I haven't seen this before. And the other two documents, P251 is an interim report which I sent to the Regional Defence Staff. It's a report on the information I had about the events in Dusina and at the Lasva junction. This last document is an order to cease all combat activities but that monitoring should be continued in accordance with the previously issued task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, at that time what sort of relations did the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff with have this area and with its subordinate units, with the anti-sabotage unit that was subordinated to it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: The main problem in the course of the war was equipment. Any equipment that was in good condition was sent to the battlefields, to the Maglaj battlefield and north-west of Zenica. Since we didn't -- we also used alternative means of communication, such as the telephone, and we could use the telephone if there was electricity and often there was no electricity. And since the combat was not dynamic, well, we expected that a courier would satisfy our needs. So one could say that we had very poor communications with them at the time, almost non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the information on the incidents and combat in that area -- or rather, in addition to the information that people had been killed and wounded on both sides, did you begin to ask yourselves whether in that territory some sort of crime had been committed too?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: At the time, there were no such reports that arrived through the regular channels. But, however, on the following day, I think, the corps command requested that these events be verified. They said that they had information according to which a crime had been committed in the Lasva Valley -- or rather, in the vicinity of the Lasva junction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have just said that the Municipal Staff did not have a military police force of its own, did you take any action when you found out that there was suspicion that some such incident had occurred?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, I contacted the Security Service and instructed them to try and find out what had happened. However, they said that the military police and the military judicial organs had already initiated a serious investigation and all we could do was follow what was being done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you first tell me what the name of your security organ was and where was it located -- or rather, who was present at the scene where this investigation was being conducted as you said?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, after they had performed the duties they were supposed to perform and joined the team that was investigating the matter - and the name of this person is Zulfikar - after he had done this, he returned and said that they had examined the bodies in the morgue. He said that the military prosecutor was up there, the military judge, military police organs, forensic experts, and other organs from the Security Services Centre, and I was very glad to hear that HVO representatives were also present. I thought that that was very revealing. I thought that if such a team was present at the scene, that they would be able to determine what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, tell me, you as the Municipal Staff commander, did you have any information about the person in charge of the investigation when the court went to the site and who would issue tasks to other organs?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, as a former officer, I knew that when the court takes things into its own hands, we shouldn't meddle in this. When any representatives of the judiciary go to the scene, the military can only assist. The investigative organs and the court do everything else, and then finally the prosecutor arrives on the scene and decides whether to take up the case or not. So when I was told about the identity of those who were present at the scene, that concluded the matter for me. I didn't want to and couldn't meddle in the affair.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, did the investigative judge ask you or your security organs -- or rather, did the military prosecutor ask you to carry out any investigations into this event?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: No, and it wouldn't have been logical for us to carry out such investigations, since we didn't have any professional organs at our disposal who could have conducted such an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you or your security organ know anything about the results of the investigations conducted, the investigations that had been ordered by the court after they had visited the scene at which the dead bodies were present is this?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: It's not the court's duty to provide me with any information, not officially at least. But unofficially, after a certain period of time had elapsed, the soldiers and officers heard that a crime had not been committed up there and we were content with that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You earlier mentioned the name of a commander of the HVO brigade. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: His name was Zivko Totic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what sort of terms were you on with Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: We were neighbours, and that's why we had very good and correct personal relationship, and we would often sit together especially in the evening and we would discuss all sorts of topics.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long did your good personal relationship last?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Well, they were never formally interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told -- you've told us that your person in charge of security informed you that members of the HVO were also involved in the investigation. Tell me whether Zivko Totic ever expressed his dissatisfaction with the investigation that had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: We very often spoke about the so-called incidents. More often than not we would realise that problems were caused by some outsiders, that they were not caused by our units. We never spoke in any great detail about this particular event. He never mentioned any problems that might have occurred with that regard. The only thing he mentioned was that he was disappointed that something like that had happened, and it was our mutual desire for this incident to just -- to be just a misfortunate concurrence of events.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you have already told us something about that, but can you please repeat. In all these discussions with the -- the HVO commander, did he ever express his suspicion that the deaths did not result as the result of combat but that they should have been the result of a crime?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: My impression was that both of us were very sorry that something like that had happened, but not for a single moment did he insinuate that this was a crime. All he said was that this was the result of fire being opened on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This joint position of your, was it identical to or different from the results of the investigation that had been carried out by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: This position was identical to what I heard were the results of the investigation, and I believe that Zivko agreed. It was an unpleasant topic which was not discussed at great length, but it seems to me that our position was more or less the same. At least, that's the impression that I gained in our contacts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, do you know what happened to Zivko Totic in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I know. I was unpleasantly surprised when his escorts were killed. And I knew these people very well. They were all my neighbours. And on that occasion Zivko Totic was kidnapped. In the Defence Staff we received this news in sheer disbelief. We were shocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the 3rd Corps do anything? Did the Municipal Staff participate in any way in those activities?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I would say that at this stage, when the corps command was being established, the corps command found this news equally shocking. An order was issued for a commission to be established, and it was the primary task of this commission to find Zivko Totic. And I believe that a set of orders was issued to that effect. My suggestion was that a representative of the staff should be involved in that team, or maybe even an order was issued to that effect. I can't remember. This person was very familiar with all the units on the ground, and he was a very respectable man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 17. This is a press statement from the command of the 3rd Corps. It bears number 0859. When you look at paragraph 3 in this press statement, would you say that it reflects your information about the reaction of the 3rd Corps to the kidnapping of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes. I have just said that the corps command was utterly shocked. We tried as best as we could to keep that relationship going, to keep it normal, and the least we wanted at the time was for an incident of this kind to happen. That is why the corps command and all members of the army were very keen on this problem being solved as soon as possible. At that time, my interest was personal because I considered Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Zivko Totic to be a very good colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Chief of Staff, did he inform you about the results of this investigation and search for Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I remember when he returned from the inspection. Wherever there was a telephone connection, he would contact me prior to that from various points. But especially when he returned, he said that he visited the places that he had never visited before and that they had looked wherever they could, both him and civilian and military police, the military police of the 3rd Corps. However, everything was to no avail; Zivko Totic was not found.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, did you find out later on who was it who had kidnapped Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: All I know about the event is that a few days later a group of Arabs contacted the European monitors who were staying in the hotel in Zenica and they wanted to negotiate with them. They wanted to negotiate about Zivko Totic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you a few questions about another topic. Were you familiar with the policy of the 3rd Corps? What was the policy of the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff of Zenica when it came to observing law?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: We were in an unpleasant situation, all of us. We were between a rock and a hard place. We didn't know what to do. However, the overall policy of the command of the 3rd Corps, once he assumed this position, was that if crimes were happening to us, we should not retaliate by committing crimes in turn. He also said that we had clear laws that prescribed the way we were supposed to behave in the times of war and that we should observe those -- those laws to the letter. If we had officially allowed our troops not to obey those basic laws, very soon we would have ended up with a chaos on our territory, and there wouldn't have been a way out of that. I know that our men were hungry. There were lots of refugees. Their houses had been destroyed. And there was a lot of pressure on the civilian authorities to deal with those problems. However, any form of plunder, any form of breaking law was prevented.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, can you look at document number 18 and also document number 22, and please tell me -- number 18 bears number 0874, and document number 22 bears number 1775. Mr. Saric, tell me whether this order, i.e., this information or this report, rather, speak in favour of what you have just told us about the strict observance of the international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: There was a standing order at the time that this should accompany every order that was issued. A little while ago you did not allow me to complete my sentence. At the time of war, we prosecuted thousands upon thousands of our men who were reported for certain crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the transcript, since the document number 22 has not been translated into English, I would kindly ask you to tell us who issued the document; what is the document number; what does it represent; and whether you recognise this document as being one of yours.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: The document was issued by the Municipal Defence Staff of Zenica. The number of this document is 14/02-29/14. The date of the document is 16 April 1993. I signed the document. This is just an overview of combat reports for a certain period of time or a summary of combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Saric, while you were the commander of the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff, you not only issued orders but also prosecuted a number of your men. Tell me, please, whether anybody could be exempted from prosecution if it was established that he had violated the law. So were there any exceptions to the prosecution rules?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: There were no exception when crimes were committed. Nobody was allowed to disobey law. We even had cases of brigade commanders who were prosecuted. I don't know whether this was in this -- during this particular period of time or later, but I can say that there were even brigade commanders who were prosecuted. Everybody without any exceptions were -- was prosecuted who had to be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a young officer, you were the commander of the Municipal Territorial Staff in a big town in a situation that was the way you described it. When you look at that situation as you sit here today, could you have done more in order to investigate and find out what happened in Dusina; and, secondly, to implement such measures that could have prevented crimes from being committed in the territory of the municipality of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: As I sit here today, I had left the JNA with the rank of captain. I had been a teacher in the military school. I had very minimum military experience. And even despite all that, I was amongst the best-educated soldiers at that time. If the corps command had not been established, I wouldn't have known what to do. I couldn't have done what I did. And I believe that at that time, when it comes to the investigation of this incident, everything was done in the same way it would be done today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Before the break, the other Defence team, do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, we don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. It is 25 to 6.00. We will make a break and we will resume at around five to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 6.00, and we have to finish by 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think there will be no problem in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Saric. My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues here, we represent the Prosecution in this case. I have just a few questions for you, sir, that relate to the questions that my learned colleague Madam Residovic asked you. Before I do so, however, sir, I would simply like to inform you that it's not my intention in any way to confuse you, and I would ask you that if you don't understand any of the questions that I ask you, just tell me and I will rephrase the question so that we're both clear and everyone is clear as to what exactly it is that we're talking about. Sir, you were asked some questions this afternoon about the time period in which the accused General Hadzihasanovic arrived in Zenica and began forming the 3rd Corps, and my question to you, sir, is: At what point in time did the Zenica Municipal TO Staff and its subordinate units become part of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: The Municipal Staff became part of the 3rd Corps by order on the formation of the 3rd Corps. However, those relations -- that structure wasn't put into effect immediately because there was a certain temporary period given the complicated situation on the battlefield and it was necessary to form a corps in the field. I'm not quite sure when the Municipal Staff terminated all relations with the War Presidency and Zenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give us, sir, an approximate time period when you began receiving orders from the commander of the 3rd Corps and reporting to the commander of the 3rd Corps, an approximate time period? Would it be the 1st of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. In any event, I received those orders from the 3rd Corps, regardless of whether they came via the Regional Staff or directly, and naturally I carried them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So at any point in time when you received orders from the 3rd Corps, you carried out those orders, irrespective of the date of a written order; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I assume so. I don't see why that shouldn't have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, of course, it would seem, sir, that if you were receiving orders and carrying out orders of the 3rd Corps, you would also be reporting to the 3rd Corps during the same time period.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: As I have just said, orders arrived from the 3rd Corps, either directly or indirectly. It was of no importance to me. The documents probably arrived in the 3rd Corps eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir: In the time period at the beginning of 1993, January, February 1993, did the Zenica District Territorial Defence Staff still exist?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: As I have said -- or as I said when I was answering questions put to me by the Defence, when the order was issued to form the 3rd Corps, the 3rd Corps was formed and its structure was established, but the District Staff remained as a temporary institution until certain elements within the 3rd Corps command had been established and men from the District Staff gradually went to the 3rd Corps command, and then a detachment for area-based units were formed and we mostly contacted the detachment that was area-based. Officers gradually changed, depending on how they were appointed posts within the corps command. So I don't see why the point when this changed is so important. I think that at that time I didn't think that that was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who was the commander of the Zenica District Defence Staff or Territorial Defence Staff in January, February 1993?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I can tell you about the identity of the commanders. I said that some left their positions. But as it was the only institution in existence, there was Mr. Dzemal Merdan who was the commander. At one point in time, he left and he was replaced by Mr. Ramiz Dugalic. And I know for sure that the last person who was in the District Staff and was then the chief of the sector for area-based units was Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you repeat the name? The interpreter apparently didn't -- didn't hear what you said, the name of the person who was chief of the sector.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Rubo [as interpreted] Hajrudin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, was there a time period, then, in early 1993 where Mr. Merdan was the commander of the Zenica District Territorial Defence Staff while at the same time he was the deputy corps commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: For a very brief period of time I think so, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, on page 66, line 23, again I think there may have been a problem with the interpreters hearing the answer. The person's name was Hubo Hajrudin; scene of an accident?-- Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Age 66 -- page 66, line 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Line 23, the name has been recorded as "Rubo Hajrudin."

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, "H," Hubo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you, sir, now a few questions about the events in Dusina, and I would like to ask you specifically about the investigation that you've told us concerning events in Dusina. It's a bit unclear to me, sir, from the English transcript, but it appears that you said that there were representatives of the HVO present or involved in this investigation. And let me ask you first of all if that's what you remember.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who these representatives were from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: There were two representatives from the Jure Francetic Brigade, but I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know at what point in the investigation these HVO representatives were involved? Did they go to the scene? Did they go to the morgue? Can you tell us about what you know about their involvement in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I have to say that all the questions you are putting to me that have to do with the investigation have no purpose. They're pointless, because I was not interested and that would have been meddling in the investigation. If I had tried to obtain more information or to do anything with regard to the investigation, that would have been meddling, since according to the laws that I had studied as a soldier, when investigative organs take over an affair, soldiers can only do what they are ordered to do and perhaps they might secure the scene or they might participate if they're ordered to participate. Nothing was ordered. I wasn't issued any orders. And I know nothing about the details of the investigation. All I could do is engage in guesswork, and I don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I -- I completely accept what you've told us, but at the same time you have testified about HVO representatives being involved in the investigation. And my only questions to you are concerning what information you have about the involvement of HVO representatives in the investigation into the incidents in Dusina on the 26th of January, 1993. At what stage in the investigation were these HVO representatives present? Where did they go? What did do? Because you've told us they were involved, and I simply want to ask you what you know about that involvement.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I obtained information on the investigation from my security officer. He told me that an investigation had been launched into the alleged crimes. I've told you how we obtained the information. He told me he was participating -- he told me about the identity of those involved in the investigation. I said I was very glad that HVO representatives -- HVO members were participating in the investigation because together with other authorised individuals, they would be in a position to determine the truth. As to where they went, what they did, as to how they conducted the investigation, I wasn't very interested in that and I didn't try to find out much about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the name of your security officer who told you this information?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Zulfikar Bojcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Bojcic or do you remember if Mr. Bojcic told you about any aspects of the investigation that was conducted in Dusina and at what point in time, if in fact he did tell you that the investigation occurred in Dusina itself?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: No. We could speak about how the commander functions, how the commander operates, how he takes decisions. At the time, we were in a very difficult and a very particular situation. It was very important to determine the fields that a commander would be involved in. It was important to rationalise the way in which time was used. From my organ of security, from my security officer, I received information that an investigation was being conducted, and after it had been conducted, I was informed that that was the case and that it wasn't necessary for us to do anything in relation to that investigation. But that was information provided by a subordinate to a superior. According to the chain of command -- or from the chain of command, from my superior command, I received no information about the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall when you had this discussion with Mr. Bojcic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, sir, you don't recall or you don't know if the investigation in Dusina took place while any of the bodies were still in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know that the bodies were transferred to the town morgue within the framework of an operation that was conducted by the town's civilian protection. I'm not sure. I don't even know whether they were transported there on the same day, on the day that they were killed. But -- well, I don't know when all this took place, nor do I know in what way the investigation was conducted. I don't know whether it was initiated up in Dusina when the individuals were there at the site. I don't know whether -- when -- I don't know whether it started in the morgue. I don't know whether -- whether anyone went to Dusina to look into the matter. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the context of the events that took place in Dusina at the end of January 1993 and in response to a question put to you by the Defence, you mentioned a discussion or discussions that you had with Zivko Totic concerning the events in Dusina. And in broad terms, you said that your discussions with Colonel Totic often centred on problems caused by outsiders. And my question, sir, is: By informing us about this discussion in the context of Dusina, were you suggesting in any way that the events in Dusina were caused by outsiders?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I'd like to tell you about the conversations we had, and I'd like to tell you that at the time I had the impression that they were quite friendly. As the Chamber probably knows, at one point in time the HVO introduced certificates which were issued by the local HVO organs throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was not possible to pass through HVO checkpoints if you didn't have such a certificate. Naturally, there were private and there were official reasons to accelerate the issuing of those certificates. It was a very laborious procedure that had to be followed if such certificates were to be obtained. On a number of occasions, I appealed -- I contacted Zivko Totic and asked him to issue certificates for certain individuals. I asked him to come and see me to issue some certificates for some individuals or for a convoy that had to leave urgently, and he was very helpful. I also helped him when it was necessary to repair some of his equipment, because when we entered the JNA barracks, there was a workshop that was well-equipped. So on the whole, the conversations we had were friendly. Since we are both born in Zenica - we are in fact neighbours - I think that the two of us tried to persuade each other that we were very sorry about what was happening there. And when certain incidents occurred at the Cajdras checkpoint that his unit controlled, he would say, "Come to" -- he would say that "people from Herzegovina appear and as soon as they appear, we have problems." So it was always our intention to maintain to the extent that it was possible normal relations in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me return to the question, sir. Are you in any way suggesting that the events in Dusina were caused by outsiders?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that is what one could claim. I can't remember what we spoke about at the time, but when we spoke about Dusina, we described it as a stupid incident that should not have occurred. And there were good examples of collaboration between the HVO and the army in Tuzla, Brcko, et cetera, and we said that we could remain on such terms too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, if you could -- I believe you still have the binder provided to you by the Defence in front of you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please turn -- could you please turn, sir, to tab 5, which is Prosecution Exhibit P310. And my learned colleague asked you some questions about this document, and you told us that you in fact drafted this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I said that I signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. That's correct. I stand corrected. You signed this document and sent it to the 3rd Corps on the 22nd of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you look, sir, in the document in your language on the fourth line, which is also the fourth line in the English translation, there's a reference to the 1st Company of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. And my question to you, sir, is: Do you recall if that 1st Company that's referred to in this document was part of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I didn't pay much attention to that. At the time, we were given a company and the military commanders would examine units. I didn't pay much attention to the battalion it was from. Perhaps it was from that battalion; perhaps not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time period, sir, that you were the commander of the District -- or the Municipal Staff, can you tell us on how many occasions other than this one a company of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade was subordinated to you.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: My unit was a local one. We were a unit that was not often in combat and it was the weakest unit. The 7th Muslim Brigade was one of the operative brigades, and in the course of the entire war it was engaged throughout the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They wouldn't be subordinated to us very frequently. Sometimes some of our elements would become part of their units. Because it was a strong unit and it was difficult for people to understand that a unit whose structure was poor would be superior to a stronger, better unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to this document you're looking at, P310, and the reference to the 1st Company of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade - excuse me - do you remember the name of the commander of that company, the 1st Company of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade that was resubordinated to your staff at that point in time in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I didn't know the name of the company commander until he was killed, but I know his surname was Camdzic and that he died in the fighting, that in fact he died in Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who replaced Camdzic as the company commander of that 1st Company?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I think the company commander and the deputy company commander were killed, and that is mentioned here in one of my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if Serif Patkovic was part of this company?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Serif Patkovic certainly wasn't a member of that company. At the time, he could only have been a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if Serif Patkovic was the commander of the battalion of which this company was part?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he was the commander of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, a few questions about Mr. Totic and his kidnapping. You told us earlier today that a few days after that kidnapping you learned that a group of Arabs, as you put it, contacted the European monitors in the hotel in Zenica. And my question, sir, is: How did you become aware of this?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: When Totic was kidnapped and his escorts were killed, that was the main subject throughout the area at the time, not only in Zenica because, as I have already said, they believed that Zenica would manage to maintain good relations between the HVO and the army, as was the case in Brcko and Tuzla, and it was believed that they would be able to act together. I have also said that I considered Zivko Totic to be a friend of mine, and he was a colleague who was a commander of a unit in town, so I was also interested in the affair. And I believe that if it could have happened to him, it could have happened to me too. If the -- if at the time I wasn't moving around with an escort, I remained in my command with a lot of security, with very tight security there. I think I received information from someone who worked with members of the European mission, but I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you -- you don't recall who told you that a group of Arabs went to the European monitors in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did Mr. Totic, if anything -- what did Mr. Totic tell you about the time he was with the people that kidnapped him? Did you ever talk to him about that afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Totic withdrew into the Vitez operation zone after that event. And we never spoke about this incident, not until after the war. He doesn't like to remember this incident, and I myself found it hard to remember. I did ask him on several occasions if he knew where he had been, but he couldn't tell me. Then I was very interested in learning who had done that, and this hasn't changed to this very day. I'm still interested in learning who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just so we're clear then, sir, Mr. Totic, your neighbour, to this day has not told you where he was or told you any of the specifics about what happened to him or told you about the people, described the people, mentioned anything to you about the people who either kidnapped him or controlled him while he was being detained by these people?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: No. I believe that a few years ago we attended a reception in Sarajevo and talked. I started the conversation along these lines and he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. only told me that this had been done by well-trained and well-equipped people, and he said that the explosion that had taken place in the vicinity was very precise and that his escorts who were killed were killed by direct fire so that nothing happened to him. He wasn't even scratched by any of the bullets. I asked him again whether he knew where he had been detained, and he only told me that there's something else who -- who should know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall on any occasion or on more than one occasion during 1993 in response to any query from Mr. Totic that you referred him to the accused General Hadzihasanovic and gave him General Hadzihasanovic's phone number in order to get more information about any subject whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me try a again. It was a bit confusing. Do you recall any occasion in 1993 where Mr. Totic contacted you about any issue and you referred him to -- to General Hadzihasanovic, even going so far as giving Mr. Totic the 3rd Corps commander's telephone number?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN SARIC
utterances.text: There's a very interesting thing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. During the war and after the war, everybody always wants to speak to number one, to the person in charge.
